lesson.title: Everyone on the Segment Hears This: Understanding Broadcast
lesson.summary: Broadcast delivers a packet to every host on a local network segment at once, using a reserved address that every device recognizes as meant for all of them, a blunt but useful tool for situations where the sender does not yet know who else is out there.
lesson.body:
Broadcast is the least selective of the delivery modes: instead of addressing a packet to one specific host, as unicast does, or to a group of hosts that opted in, as multicast does, a broadcast packet is addressed to every host on the local network segment, whether or not they have any interest in it. IPv4 supports this through reserved broadcast addresses. Within any given subnet, the highest address in the range, 192.168.1.255 in a 192.168.1.0/24 network for instance, serves as that subnet's broadcast address, and the special address 255.255.255.255 serves as a limited broadcast meaning simply everyone on this local link. Crucially, broadcast packets stay confined to their local broadcast domain, since routers do not forward them onward by default the way they forward unicast and multicast traffic, so broadcast traffic never floods the wider internet.

The DHCP boot process is the example that makes broadcast's purpose obvious. When a laptop joins a network for the first time, it has no IP address yet, and without an IP address it cannot address a unicast packet to a specific DHCP server because it does not know that server's address either. It has a genuine chicken-and-egg problem. The laptop resolves this by sending a DHCPDISCOVER message to the broadcast address 255.255.255.255. Every device on the local segment receives and can inspect that packet, but only the DHCP server actually acts on it, replying with an offer of an IP address. Broadcast is exactly the right tool here because the sender does not yet know, and cannot yet ask, who the right recipient even is.

This same logic explains why broadcast exists at all in the network layer: it is reserved for situations of genuine ambiguity or bootstrapping, discovering unknown neighbors, distributing information no host can be assumed to already have a specific address for, or reaching everyone when reaching everyone actually is the intent. It is deliberately not the default, because every host on the segment has to spend processing time inspecting broadcast traffic whether it needs it or not, and a network flooded with unnecessary broadcasts, sometimes called a broadcast storm, can degrade performance for every device sharing that segment.

It is also worth noting that IPv6 dropped broadcast entirely, folding its use cases into a more disciplined use of multicast, since IPv6's designers judged that most broadcast use cases were really reach a well-known group problems in disguise, better solved without forcing every host on the link to process traffic it had no interest in.

The Address Resolution Protocol, ARP, offers another everyday broadcast example, though it technically operates just below the network layer. When a host on a LAN knows another device's IP address but needs to learn its hardware address before it can actually deliver a frame, it sends an ARP request to the Ethernet broadcast address, so every host on the segment receives and inspects the request, even though only the one host whose IP address matches will ever reply, and it replies directly with an ordinary unicast frame. That pattern, broadcasting a question because the specific answerer is not yet known, and getting a targeted unicast reply once it is, echoes the same bootstrapping logic seen in DHCP.
